Players take turns placing orbs on a grid; when a cell reaches critical mass it explodes into its neighbors, converting their orbs and often triggering cascading chain reactions. The objective is to eliminate every opponent orb from the board. The app supports human vs. human, human vs. computer, and computer vs. computer with human interaction, and tracks a live scoreboard throughout the game. It is hosted on Firebase and playable in any browser."), "\n", React.createElement(_components.h2, null, "The Game"), "\n", React.createElement(_components.p, null, "Chain Reaction is a deterministic, perfect-information combinatorial game for two to eight players — no dice, no hidden state, yet remarkably unpredictable in practice. The board is an ", React.createElement(_components.em, null, "m × n"), " grid (typically 9 × 6). Each cell has a critical mass equal to its number of orthogonally adjacent cells: 4 for interior cells, 3 along the edges, and 2 in the corners."), "\n", React.createElement(_components.p, null, "Players take turns placing an orb in an empty cell or one that already holds their own orbs. When a cell's orb count reaches its critical mass, it explodes: it loses orbs equal to its critical mass and sends one orb to each orthogonally adjacent cell. Any opponent orbs in those cells are converted to the exploding player's color, which can set off further explosions — a chain reaction that continues until every cell is stable. A player is out once they lose all of their orbs."), "\n", React.createElement(_components.h2, null, "Heuristic Strategy"), "\n", React.createElement(_components.p, null, "A player's score is the total number of orbs they hold on the board. Each move expands into a modified DFS/BFS over the board to compute the resulting state, and that expansion happens for every candidate move at every layer of the Minimax tree. On a 5 × 5 board a player can have ~25 possible moves; at a search depth of 3 that is roughly ", React.createElement(_components.code, null, "n³"), " move combinations, and if each state evaluation costs about ", React.createElement(_components.code, null, "n⁴"), ", the worst case approaches ", React.createElement(_components.code, null, "O(n⁶)"), " — dangerously slow."), "\n", React.createElement(_components.p, null, "The key observation was that the same board states recur constantly across the search.   }, "const memorize = new Map<string, any>();\n\n//memorize node and actions\nfunction actions(node: Node): IAction[] {\n    let key = JSON.stringify(node);\n    if (memorize.has(key)) {\n        return memorize.get(key);\n    }\n    // Computation\n}\n\nasync function result(action: IAction, node: Node): Promise<Node> {\n    let key = JSON.stringify(node) + JSON.stringify(action);\n    if (memorize.has(key)\n    )\n        return memorize.get(key);\n// Computation\n}\n\n// memorize\nfunction maxValue(node: Node): number {\n    const key = JSON.stringify(node);\n    if (memorize.has(key)) {\n        return memorize.get(key);\n    }\n    // Computation\n}\n\n//memorize\nfunction minValue(node: Node): number {\n  let key = JSON.stringify(node);\n  if (memorize.has(key)) {\n    return memorize.get(key);\n  }\n  // Computation\n}\n")), "\n", React.createElement(_components.h2, null, "Conclusion"), "\n", React.createElement(_components.p, null, "Chain Reaction brings a classic strategy game to the web and pairs it with a Minimax AI that plays a genuinely challenging game. The most interesting engineering problem was performance: a direct search is exponentially expensive, and memoizing recurring game states was what made a depth-3 AI responsive enough to play in real time. The result is a polished, browser-based game and a practical case study in applying game-theory algorithms under real performance constraints."));
